sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

content.text:
Case V25: segment the vascular soft-tissue tumor on this T2-weighted MRI.

Volume: 501x501x283 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case V25 | sequence T2 | shape (i,j,k)=(501, 501, 283) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: vascular soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).
axial 141/283 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 1/40, prompts 0/15

I'm noting the axial dimensions at 501x501 with 283 slices, and the coronal view appears compressed vertically, so I'll examine it across multiple sheets.

content.thinking:
I notice the marks seem to avoid the lesion area entirely, which is strange — maybe the mark generator intentionally excludes it. I'm trying to pin down coordinates for a bounding box, estimating the mass spans roughly x 290-500, y 155-300 in the left panel, translating to around x 1074 onward in the right panel.

Testing a few corner combinations, but each box I construct either clips part of the mass or ends up far larger than the mass itself, which risks the model segmenting surrounding tissue instead of the tumor. A tight lasso polygon around the mass using nearby marks would also end up oversized. I'm starting to think a different slice might have marks that actually fall inside the mass, suggesting these points could be chosen in 3D rather than per-slice.

Since the mass appears to be one of the uniform regions marked with a single centroid point, I'm trying to locate which slice contains that centroid — estimating axial, coronal, and sagittal indices by converting the mass's pixel position back to voxel coordinates using the panel scaling factor, though I'm not fully certain about the orientation convention being used.

None of the marks land inside the mass even with finer crops, so maybe the generator avoids placing triangles directly on the lesion, or edge detection just isn't picking up its low-gradient border. Given the time budget and only 8 of 40 calls used, I should try a different axial slice efficiently rather than keep refining the same one.

A box prompt might also oversegment past the object boundary, so that's risky too. A lasso polygon on the 164 crop covers most of the mass but drags in extra dark tissue to the right, which could confuse the model since lasso regions get filled in as-is. I think checking a sagittal slice through the mass center might reveal marks closer to the lesion — ideally the 3D "centre of uniform region" triangle should land right at the mass center if I can find the correct slice.

Trying that box gives a mass of 222x205 inside a 670x248 region, which is too loose a fit. Switching to the coronal crop, I check marks near the mass boundaries but they're all too far from the actual lesion location. I think I need to zoom in further on marks closer to the mass itself to get a tighter crop.

Since zooming on isolated id pairs still gives roughly the same loose bounding box, I'm considering instead just painting a polygon directly over the marks on the current slice and applying it across the relevant slice range as a more direct segmentation edit.

A scribble connecting marks through the mass would also cross non-mass tissue on both sides, which would wrongly include that tissue in a positive scribble — so that approach seems flawed. I'm now wondering whether checking the sagittal view might reveal marks lying on that plane instead, since the same 3D points should appear wherever their slice coincides across views.

Maybe the mass simply has no 3D marks on it at all except edge marks, and the current crop only captured strong edges elsewhere. A tighter crop focused closer to the mass boundary itself might surface edge marks I'm missing, so I should try picking different id combinations to shift the crop center and checking other axial slices for marks near the mass.

I think I'll switch strategies and sweep through sagittal slices with a coarse grid to locate the mass's sagittal index, then rerun with coarse marks once I find it.

content.thinking:
I'm burning through calls without hitting the mass—none of my marks (E2, E40, 1543, 1848, E35, 1304, 1375) land in the target region spanning roughly x 1043-1172, y 135-235 in the right panel. I should try a box or lasso approach using the axial crop to get closer to the mass boundaries instead of continuing with isolated point marks.

The interactive box would segment the dominant bright object, likely the mass, though it might leak onto the nearby ring structure that could be a vessel or bowel segment. I'm weighing whether a loose box plus negative points to clean up leaks would work better than a tighter polygon, since the leak-prone areas align with where the marks cluster anyway.

Now I'm trying to figure out the exact box coordinates for both the sagittal and coronal views, checking whether a given box corner-to-corner span actually covers the mass's full extent in x and y without missing edges or including too much of the surrounding bright structures below it.

Converting at full axial scale, the mass spans roughly 95mm wide, but a bounding box tight enough to capture it would still run 268mm across — too wide to be useful. Trying to hug the mass edge with fine marks doesn't work either, since those marks only appear on bright tissue and aren't present along the lesion boundary itself.

Maybe cropping could limit edge detection to a region excluding the dominant bright body wall, letting the mass boundary become the strongest edge — but all the available marks sit in bright areas, so this constraint is hard to satisfy. Looking at the sagittal view, the nearest marks to the mass don't line up well either.

I also wonder if a different axial slice with the ring/vessel structure nearby could help, but that region had no marks in my earlier view. I think the simplest path is to try a box crop and correct from there rather than attempting a polygon lasso with incomplete vertices.

Looking at view 7's coronal marks, I'm trying to locate the mass within the right panel coordinates and comparing a candidate bounding box against the mass dimensions — the box comes out roughly 5x larger in area than the mass itself, so I'll need to tighten it considerably.

Thinking through the sagittal views too, the mass seems centered around slice 205. I should pull up the axial crop view again to cross-reference the segmentation marks before drawing a tighter bounding box.

A box would cut off the mass bottom-right, so that's worse than a lasso here. I'm weighing whether paint-plus-refine could work instead, but refining from a rough over-segmentation likely won't tighten precisely to the mass, so I'll stick with box coordinates and check which corner pairs give the tightest fit without cutting the mass edges, trying a few crop id combinations to see if better marks appear.

content.thinking:
I'm checking the coordinates for several candidate bounding boxes and a lasso polygon in the right panel, trying to find one that tightly matches the mass's actual dimensions rather than being too loose.

I try another lasso path, but it still cuts into the mass bottom by roughly 20mm, which isn't precise enough. content.thinking:
That 1522 mL result was wrong since it segmented the whole box region, so I'm undoing that and reconsidering. The model seems to be taking the box prompt too literally, so I need a different approach to prompting — maybe using the existing mask to crop with a 'mask' view to see if finer marks reveal themselves within it, though I'm unsure whether that captures the dark, uniform regions properly.

Fine marks seem to only appear on bright areas, not within the dark mass, so that approach won't work either. I'm thinking about combining paint and erase: painting a rough polygon around the mass using far-apart marks as vertices, then carving away the excess with erase polygons, since straight lines between distant marks could still pass close to the mass boundary and approximate its shape through intersecting half-planes.

I'm also weighing positive scribbles drawn between two marks across the mass, but that risks including non-mass tissue along the path unless I pair it with negative points. And I'm reconsidering the box prompt option — since the earlier box was much larger than the actual mass and still got fully segmented, maybe a tighter box, even if imperfect, could work better than these polygon workarounds.

Another angle: seg_candidates could propose the mass itself if I first place a small mask adjacent to or touching it, since candidates often surface nearby bright homogeneous regions the current mask missed — then seg_accept and refine from there. But I'd need to construct that touching mask first, since starting from an empty mask after undo gives no candidates to work with.

Alternatively, I'm reconsidering the sagittal plane crop, since the mass there occupies a specific region with mostly dark surroundings, but the reference marks only sit along the periphery, so a bounding box there would end up far too large to be useful.

I'm reconsidering whether 1245 itself falls in the bright wall region, which would explain the confusion. The edge numbering (E1-E34 but only ~14 shown) suggests edges are computed across the full slice then filtered to the crop region, which could explain why some marks seem to disappear. I should try a different approach to isolate edges actually on the mass.

Maybe instead I should look at the candidates approach — something that automatically proposes lesion tissue the current mask might be missing, based purely on image intensity. That might threshold intensity near the mask's own values and find nearby connected regions, since I can't paint directly inside the mass but could seed from the mask's boundary.

I'm also weighing whether a painted polygon spanning the mass plus some surrounding tissue would just mix up the mask's intensity statistics too much to be useful, versus trying to erase non-mass regions from the v1 box result, which seems overly complex given the irregular boundaries. Another option is negative prompting — placing negative points or scribbles on the obviously non-mass tissue around it, like the bright left region or ring structure, though the dark region on the right has no existing marks to build from.

Now I'm checking whether a negative lasso could work, since it requires at least three ordered marks forming a closed polygon to exclude an inside region, but the available marks are still too far from the mass boundary to form a tight exclusion zone. I'm now scanning the coronal full view instead, looking at the marks positioned around the mass's x/y coordinates there to see if they'd form a better-fitting box or lasso.

Checking the sagittal full view marks against the mass coordinates, none form a tight box either—the nearby marks are scattered too far to bound the region cleanly. I'm wondering if I should look at other slices near the mass periphery, where marks might sit adjacent to the structure, rather than trying to force a bounding box from the current crop.

Opening v1 with a large radius won't help since it's already one big blob. A paint-based approach seems more promising: start with an empty mask, add a polygon approximating the mass across a slice range, then let refine snap the boundary to the actual structure—though I need to consider how shape changes across slices might affect that refinement in 3D.

A single-slice paint prompt might still propagate to a full 3D segmentation if nnInteractive treats the mask as a 3D prior, but I'm uncertain how reliably that works. I'm also weighing whether a lasso prompt behaves like the box tool did—carving out a literal filled region rather than conforming to the mass boundary.

Looking more closely at where marks fall relative to the mass across axial, coronal, and sagittal views, I'm trying to figure out if these triangle marks represent centers of uniform supervoxel regions, and whether the mass itself—being fairly uniform—might have its own center mark on a slice I haven't checked yet. I should look for whether a mark appears near the mass's estimated 3D centroid on nearby slices, since the current slice's marks are all too far away.

Given no nearby marks exist, I'm now considering drawing a polygon directly on the current axial 164 view to approximate the mass boundary, since that view should still be active after the previous box operation—though I need to undo the earlier call first before painting.

I need a line passing right along the mass's left edge, so I'm checking marks above and below at x≈1146 to see which pairs of points form a line close enough to that boundary. Testing a few candidate lines between top and bottom marks, I keep landing 50-100px too far left of the actual edge.

Continuing the boundary estimates, I find the right edge lands around x≈1290-1316 depending on y, so overall the polygon approximation is off from the actual mass by roughly 10-25 px, or about 7-16mm. I'll need to refine this with a 3D prism model spanning slices 135-190, since the mass shape shifts across slices.

Since I can only build polygons from existing marks, not arbitrary lines, I'm thinking through how to approximate a quadrilateral: I could add one large polygon then erase four half-plane regions, each erase-polygon having one edge as the cutting line and the rest extending outward past the mass boundary.

I'm reconsidering whether a self-intersecting polygon could help, since with even-odd fill rules, crossed edges can create holes or filled regions depending on winding order — like a pentagram's center behaving as a hole, or a bowtie quadrilateral creating alternating filled zones. I'm trying to figure out if ordering the vertices in a crossed sequence could isolate just the mass region.

Trying a crossed-path chain doesn't quite work geometrically — each candidate vertex ends up too far from the mass to connect naturally. Maybe the right structure is pentagram-like, where five outer vertices connect via crossing edges so the inner region forms a pentagon with even-odd winding creating a hole.

So the approach would be: draw a big convex polygon over the mass in add mode, then erase with the pentagram shape to cut away the five triangular points, leaving the central pentagon plus leftover regions outside the star. Those leftover regions between star points would need removing separately, perhaps via a component-keeping step, since the center pentagon stays connected to the surrounding star points.

This path is getting overly complicated, so I want to step back and consider whether seg_candidates could just propose the mass region directly based on intensity, which would be a much simpler route.

Another thought: instead of erasing/keep_component tricks, maybe I should look at marks on other slices where the mass is smaller and more isolated — near the top and bottom of its axial range, or in the coronal view where nearby structures might have usable marks close to the mass boundary.

Given the time I've spent, I should move faster: I'll undo and check axial 185 with coarse marks, and if any mark lands inside the mass, use it directly as a point prompt.

content.thinking:
I notice the marks only appear in the bright subcutaneous body wall regions, suggesting the generator treats the dark interior as background and never places marks there. This makes me think a box-based approach might be interpreted differently by the model, essentially filling the whole specified region rather than respecting tissue boundaries.

Painting a rough polygon around the mass and then erasing or refining seems like a more promising path, though candidates alone won't help distinguish the mass from surrounding tissue. I'm weighing whether to work from the axial slice where the mass is largest versus a smaller cross-section, and considering whether a crude prism spanning a slice range could be refined afterward rather than trying to get the polygon exactly right upfront. I'm also still turning over whether a self-intersecting polygon with tangent edges could isolate the central region using even-odd fill logic.

Thinking through star-polygon winding numbers now — a heptagram leaves the outer points filled even if the center isn't, which doesn't solve the problem. I consider instead painting a convex shape over the mass and then erasing with a pentagram-shaped cutout, since even-odd fill would leave the inner pentagon (the mass) untouched while removing the star points, but leftover fragments outside the star within the original shape would still need cleanup via morphological opening to disconnect them, keeping only the central connected component.

This gets complicated since I'd need five marks positioned so the pentagram's inner pentagon precisely matches the mass's footprint, but the available marks are clustered to the left and right rather than evenly spaced. A simpler approach is to use the left-side and right-side mark clusters to form roughly horizontal lines tangent to the mass's top and bottom edges, while separate top and bottom marks on the right side could provide near-vertical tangent lines for the mass's left and right edges.

I'm trying different pairings of these marks and tracing where each resulting line crosses the mass's height, but the intersections keep landing either too far left or cutting diagonally through the mass itself rather than staying tangent to its edge, so none of the combinations tried so far actually work cleanly.

I'm reconsidering the approach: a box with negative points won't help since there's no marks in the dark interior tissue to use as negatives—all marks are confined to the body wall. A lasso has the same limitation, and seg_candidates on the box region doesn't seem productive either. Maybe I should accept a partial solution: use a box or lasso in a plane where it's tight in two dimensions and let the model infer the third.

Actually I'm noticing the v1 result had a z-extent of 73-257, far larger than the mass itself—so that approach overshot badly. Thinking more about seg_candidates: it proposes regions matching the mask's intensity, so if my mask were a small chunk mostly within the mass, the candidates might fill in the rest, but I can't place marks inside the mass directly. Maybe a thin sliver or triangle crossing horizontally through the mass center, touching non-mass tissue on both sides, could work better.

I keep running into the problem that vertices define marks along a single polyline, so I can't mix positive and negative within the same crossing line to isolate just the mass. I'm wondering if a positive scribble through a different plane, where the mass is the only distinct structure crossed, might avoid picking up the dark interior and ring structure.

I'm second-guessing whether a positive scribble over dark tissue would even give a clean segmentation — it might produce something odd. Shifting to think about which viewing plane yields the best polygon shape: for sagittal 205, the mass sits in a specific coordinate range, and I'm cataloging the various marked points around it to figure out which ones actually bound the region versus which are extraneous edge markers.

Now I'm checking coronal 290 similarly, mapping out the left-column and right-side marks around the mass coordinates, along with top and bottom markers, to see if this plane gives a more complete bounding set than sagittal did.

content.text:
I saved a mask for case V25 with medium confidence. It covers the whole tumor, but it also includes a strip of normal tissue on the patient's right side that I couldn't remove.

**The lesion:** a large, smooth, evenly bright mass in the middle of the body. It runs about axial slices 127–197 and measures roughly 9 × 8.5 × 7 cm.

**The final mask (v14):** 366.6 mL, extending axial 127–197, coronal 242–332, sagittal 162–279. There is one main piece plus a tiny stray fragment of almost no volume. In the final review, the slices just past each end of the mask show no tumor left out. The sagittal outline follows the tumor edge closely.

**Why I couldn't prompt the model directly:** the tool placed no pointing marks inside or near the mass, in any plane or zoom, including edge marks. Marks appeared only in the bright tissue along the left and right sides of the body. That ruled out a point on the tumor. A box between those far-off marks made the model fill the whole box (1,523 mL), so I undid it. I built the mask another way instead:
1. Painted a rough four-sided outline around the mass and trimmed it with erase polygons.
2. Let the model clean up the boundary, then removed thin attached bits with a morphological opening.
3. Cut away extra tissue with straight lines drawn between distant marks, then let the model smooth the result once more.

**Remaining problems:**
- **Extra tissue on the patient's right (image left):** a band roughly 1–2 cm wide is still included, along with a small bulge at axial 180. No line through the available marks could cut it off without slicing into the tumor. So the mask probably overstates the volume; my rough size estimate puts the tumor nearer 300–350 mL.
- **Small cuts at the edges:** the straight cut on the patient's left and the one along the front edge may each trim a few millimetres off the tumor. The final model pass appeared to restore some of this.

The tool calls ran out before any more trimming was possible.
